Time series part 2

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/time-series-analysis-and-forecasting/

time series plot means plotting data against time. for components of time series refe https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/data-science/components-of-time-series-data/

A seasonal pattern exists when a series is influenced by seasonal factors (e.g., the quarter of the year, the month, or day of the week). Seasonality is always of a fixed and known period. Hence, seasonal time series are sometimes called periodic time series.

A cyclic pattern exists when data exhibit rises and falls that are not of fixed period.

Linear filtering is the process of transforming a time series into another time series by taking linear combinations of its current and past values. Mathematically, a linear filter can be written as:

\[ y_t=\sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty a_k x_{t-k} \]

Purpose Filter Type Description
Smoothing Moving average Reduces random noise to show underlying trend
Detrending Differencing Removes trend (acts as a high-pass filter)
Seasonal adjustment Seasonal difference Removes repeating seasonal patterns
Lag operator AR/MA models Represented as filters that depend on lagged terms

Time series smoothing

simple moving average SMA= sum of last n values / n

“Imagine you track your daily step count. Some days you walk 12,000 steps, others only 3,000. It jumps up and down — hard to see the pattern. But if you take the average of the last 7 days every day, the number changes more smoothly — that’s a 7-day moving average!”

“Imagine you’re walking uphill — your altitude keeps rising. Instead of tracking your altitude, what if you record how much you moved up or down each step? The resulting values might fluctuate around zero — that’s differencing.”

log_ap <- log(AirPassengers)
plot(log_ap, main="Log(AirPassengers)", col="steelblue")

diff_ap <- diff(log_ap,1)
plot(diff_ap, main = "1st Difference of log(AirPassengers)", col = "darkred")

diff_ap <- diff(log_ap,2)
plot(diff_ap, main = "2st Difference of log(AirPassengers)", col = "darkred")

diff_ap <- diff(log_ap,3)
plot(diff_ap, main = "3st Difference of log(AirPassengers)", col = "darkred")

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(log_ap, main="Log(AirPassengers)", col="steelblue")
plot(diff(log_ap), main="1st Differenced log(AirPassengers)", col="darkred")

par(mfrow=c(1,1))
diff_seasonal <- diff(log_ap, lag = 12)
plot(diff_seasonal, main = "Seasonally Differenced log(AirPassengers)", col = "purple")

Additive seasonality occurs when the magnitude of seasonal fluctuations is relatively constant over time, like a steady up-and-down pattern. Multiplicative seasonality occurs when the magnitude of seasonal fluctuations increases or decreases proportionally with the trend of the data, meaning the peaks and troughs get wider or narrower as the overall level of the series changes

In an additive model, the observed value is the sum of trend, seasonality, and residual components: Y(t) = Trend(t) + Seasonality(t) + Residual(t).

A multiplicative model represents the observed value as the product of its components: Y(t) = Trend(t) * Seasonality(t) * Residual(t).

data("co2")
plot(co2)

decompose_co2<-decompose(co2)
print(decompose_co2)

STL stands for Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess.

It’s a flexible, nonparametric method that works especially well for data with:nonlinear trends, and changing seasonality.It’s available in base R — no extra package required!

https://www.datascienceinstitute.net/ai-data-science-blog/time-series-decomposition-in-r

log_ap <- log(AirPassengers)
stl_ap <- stl(log_ap, s.window = "periodic")
# periodic means constant season
plot(stl_ap)

stl_ap2 <- stl(log_ap, s.window = 13, t.window = 25, robust = TRUE)
plot(stl_ap2)

library(forecast)
## Registered S3 method overwritten by 'quantmod':
##   method            from
##   as.zoo.data.frame zoo
fit <- stl(log_ap, s.window="periodic")
fcast <- forecast(fit)
plot(fcast)

The Intuitive Meaning of “Level”

The level of a time series is simply its baseline value — the underlying “average” around which the data fluctuates at a given point in time.

Think of it as the current overall position or height of the series, ignoring trend or seasonality.

Analogy:

Imagine a tide on the beach:

The waves going up and down = seasonality

  • The slowly rising sea due to climate = trend

    The current waterline right now = level

  • So, the level is the “center” or “baseline” value of the time series at time t.

    https://byjus.com/maths/exponential-smoothing/

Holt–Winters Exponential Smoothing

  • Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) → handles level (no trend or seasonality)

  • Holt’s Linear Method → handles level + trend

  • Holt–Winters Method → handles level + trend + seasonality

So Winter’s smoothing is the natural next step — it extends exponential smoothing to include seasonal effects in addition to trend and level.

“Winter’s method continuously updates estimates of three components:

the current level (ℓₜ), the trend or growth rate (bₜ), and the seasonal pattern (sₜ).”

Component Updated Equation Controlled by
level \((\ell t = \alpha y_t + (1 - \alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}))\) \(\alpha\)
trend \((b_t = \beta\^(\ell*t -* \ell\_{t-1}) + (1 - \beta\^)b\_{t-1})\) \(\beta\)
Seasonality \((s_t = \gamma(y_t - \ell*t) + (1 -* \gamma)s{t-m})\) \(\gamma\)
Forecast \(\hat{y}_{t+h}\) \(\ell t + h b_t + s{t+h-m(k)}\)
Method Captures Level Captures Trend Captures Seasonality R Function
Simple Exponential Smoothing ✅ ❌ ❌ HoltWinters(y, beta=FALSE, gamma=FALSE)
Holt’s Linear Method ✅ ✅ ❌ HoltWinters(y, gamma=FALSE)
Holt–Winters ✅ ✅ ✅ HoltWinters(y)

Errors should be random (no patterns), symmetric and consistent

ACF (auto correlation function) plot

  • auto indicates itself

  • Errors should be random (no patterns)

  • Errors should be symmetric (Around 0) histogram should be more at 0 (mean and median is zero)

  • Error should be same size over time (plot errors over time) fennel effet errors are gradually increasing

– step change =sudden change in error rate.

https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/311446_08b00d63cc794e158b1f4763eb70d43a.html

Similarity Search in Time-Series Data

To measure how similar or different two time series are — even if they vary in speed or timing.

Example

Imagine two people walking along the same route:

Person A walks steadily.

Person B walks slowly at first and faster later.

Their paths (shapes of their time series) are the same, but their timing differs.
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/similarity-search-for-time-series-data/

Traditional distance metrics like Euclidean distance would say they’re different because it compares point-to-point in time.

DTW (Dynamic Time Warping) solves this.

Dynamic Time Warping allows non-linear alignment between two time series.

It “warps” (stretches or compresses) the time axis to find the best possible match. So instead of comparing each time point \(t_1\), \(t_2\), \(t_3\), … directly, DTW aligns them flexibly.
